subject: ophthalmology
title: Diseases of the eyelids

steps.tx: **Blepharitis** inflames the lid margins in anterior and posterior patterns. Anterior disease splits into staphylococcal ulcerative disease with collarettes and lash loss and seborrhoeic disease with scales. Posterior disease reflects **meibomian gland dysfunction** with capped orifices and frothy tears and links with rosacea. Chronicity breeds styes, chalazia, marginal keratitis and dry eye. Management starts with lid hygiene using compresses that melt meibum with scrubs and massage, adds antibiotics for flares and uses systemic doxycycline or azithromycin for posterior disease. Dandruff at lash bases flags Demodex mites needing tea tree care.
steps.say: Blepharitis is the inflammation that crusts the lid margins and it returns again and again without daily care. Anterior disease coats the lashes with collarettes or greasy scales and is marked by lashes shed over time. Posterior disease caps the oil glands and is recognised by frothy tears, often alongside rosacea of the face. Warm compresses with scrubs and massage melt the oils first, antibiotics calm infective flares and selected patients need oral treatment. Cylindrical dandruff around lash bases means mites and needs tea tree based care.

steps.tx: Gland lumps separate by pain and wall. **Hordeolum externum** forms a painful staphylococcal abscess of the lash follicle or Zeiss gland at the margin. **Hordeolum internum** strikes meibomian glands and points inward through conjunctiva. Both settle with heat and drain, with incision reserved for pointing persistence. **Chalazion** forms a chronic painless sterile lipogranuloma of a meibomian gland with a tarsal nodule and conjunctival granuloma. It starts conservatively, then accepts steroid injection or incision and curettage through conjunctiva. Recurrent or atypical chalazion in older adults needs histology to exclude sebaceous carcinoma.
steps.say: A painful lump at the lid margin behaves like an abscess and it points outward through the skin. A painful lump deeper in the lid points inward and it drains through the conjunctiva. Both settle with sustained heat and they usually burst on their own. A painless firm nodule that lingers for weeks is a chalazion, which starts with heat and massage and later accepts steroid or curettage. A recurrent or odd chalazion in an older adult deserves a biopsy because cancer can masquerade.

vis.caption: Eyelid lumps: stye (hordeolum) vs. chalazion

steps.tx: Lid malpositions threaten cornea through exposure or lash trauma. **Entropion** turns the margin inward in involutional disease from laxity with retractor disinsertion, cicatricial disease from trachoma or burns, spastic disease after surgery and congenital forms. **Ectropion** everts the margin in involutional disease with punctal eversion and watering, paralytic disease from facial palsy and cicatricial forms. Trichiasis misdirects lashes while distichiasis adds a row, and both abrade cornea toward ulcers. Epilation buys time while electrolysis, cryotherapy or surgery cures. Palsy with lagophthalmos needs taping with lubricants and gold weight or tarsorrhaphy.
steps.say: Inturned lids scrape the cornea with every blink and they invite ulcers and scars. Involutional entropion follows lax tissues with a detached retractor, while scarring from trachoma or burns drags the margin inward. Outturned lids expose the surface and they spill tears over the cheek, especially after facial palsy. Misdirected or extra lashes need removal and the lid needs definitive surgery, while a palsied eye needs taping with lubricants and often a weight.

steps.tx: This close photo shows **involutional entropion** with the lower lid rolling inward so lashes brush the cornea. Labels mark **horizontal laxity** with a loose lid and the inset diagram shows retractor disinsertion that lets the margin flip. The combination explains why age related entropion waters, irritates and ulcerates the cornea. The image teaches the exam mechanism of laxity plus disinsertion and points toward lid tightening with retractor repair. Spotting lash cornea touch should trigger urgent lid assessment.
steps.say: This photo shows an aged lower lid rolling inward with lashes sweeping the cornea. Loose horizontal tissues let the margin drift and a detached retractor lets it flip fully inward. The eye waters constantly and the cornea is exposed to scratches and ulcers with every blink. Lid tightening with retractor repair corrects the mechanism, so lash cornea touch is referred promptly.

steps.tx: **Ptosis** droops the upper lid with margin reflex distance under 2 mm. Aponeurotic disease shows a high crease with preserved levator function, myogenic disease weakens the levator and neurogenic disease includes third nerve palsy with Horner syndrome with miosis and anhidrosis. Levator resection suits fair function while frontalis sling bypasses poor function in congenital disease and Marcus Gunn jaw winking. The commonest malignancy is **basal cell carcinoma** of the lower lid with a pearly rolled edge and telangiectasia, excised with margin control. Sebaceous carcinoma mimics recurrent chalazion and demands biopsies.
steps.say: A drooping upper lid with a low margin distance signals ptosis and levator testing guides the operation. Good levator function suits resection while poor function needs a frontalis sling, especially in congenital droop and jaw winking. A third nerve palsy turns the eye down and out while Horner syndrome shrinks the pupil and dries sweating. A pearly lower lid ulcer with surface vessels behaves like basal cell cancer and needs excision with margin control, while a recurrent chalazion in an older adult warns of sebaceous cancer.
